lessons.title: Welcome: your pathway and the shared Lab header

cues.intro: In lesson one, you're going to use the shared header and check that the same C Ionian setting carries between the labs.
cues.explain-a: At the top of the screen, choose C as the root, Major as the family and Ionian as the mode. Ionian is another name for the major scale. Select guitar and Shape two. Keep the displayed fingerings unchanged.
cues.explain-b: Use both directions over two octaves at sixty BPM. BPM means beats per minute. The settings control the scale and its playback speed. Listening to the example is enough for this lesson. You don't need to play the full scale yet.
cues.check: Find the root and tempo controls. Check which chooses the starting note and which changes the playback speed. Pluck one open string and listen as the sound fades.
cues.to-lab: Open Mode Lab. Select C as the root, Major family, Ionian mode, guitar and Shape two. Use both directions over two octaves at sixty BPM. Visit the seven labs in the lesson and check that each shows C Ionian.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen. Review the lab names and find the root and tempo controls. Open one lab at a time, then return to the lesson.
cues.in-lab: Visit each of the seven labs and check C Ionian. Choose one control in each lab and note what it changes. Keep the guitar supported while using the screen. Leave playback stopped until the settings have been checked.
cues.back: Review the root and mode shown in each lab. Correct any setting that differs from C Ionian before continuing.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, revisit two labs for practice.
cues.retry: If a lab shows a different root or mode, return to the header. Select C and Ionian, then check that lab again.
cues.wrap: Spend five minutes revisiting two labs. Keep the tempo at sixty BPM and check C Ionian in each. Next, compare acoustic guitar, electric guitar and bass sounds.

lessons.title: History: why the twin instruments exist

cues.intro: In lesson two, you're going to compare acoustic guitar, electric guitar and bass, then name each instrument from its sound.
cues.explain-a: An acoustic guitar uses its vibrating strings, bridge and body to move the air. An electric guitar usually uses pickups and an amplifier to make that small string signal loud enough for a room. Neither instrument belongs to just one style.
cues.explain-b: Electric guitars developed as players needed more volume. The electric bass brought a fretted, amplified option to the bass role. A standard four string bass is tuned like the guitar's four lowest strings, but an octave lower. Effects and playing style can change all these sounds.
cues.check: Listen to each example twice. Describe its pitch range and attack, then select the instrument name.
cues.to-lab: Stay in Study Lab. Compare the clean instrument examples one at a time. Describe the range and attack before choosing the name.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Review the instrument descriptions here. Describe the range and sound of each instrument from a recording you know. Return to the labelled examples before taking the listening test.
cues.in-lab: Keep playback at a comfortable volume. Compare pitch range and attack rather than loudness alone. Use the clean examples before comparing processed sounds. Replay each example before selecting an answer if needed.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, the parts of the guitar.
cues.retry: Effects can hide the instrument sound. Replay the clean reference and compare the lowest notes and the start of each sound.
cues.wrap: Spend three minutes comparing the clean examples. No metronome is needed. Name the instrument and describe one audible difference. Next, study the instrument parts.

lessons.title: The Instrument: parts and how it sounds

cues.intro: In lesson three, you're going to name the main guitar parts and follow how a vibrating string makes sound.
cues.explain-a: Look at the whole instrument. The body is the large part. The neck carries the fretboard. At the end is the headstock, with the tuning machines. Follow one string from its tuning machine, across the nut, along the neck and down to the bridge.
cues.explain-b: Now look at how sound starts. You pluck a string and it vibrates. On an acoustic, the bridge transfers vibration into the soundboard. On an electric, magnetic pickups sense the movement of suitable strings. The cable carries that signal towards an amplifier.
cues.check: Find the nut and bridge without labels. State which end of the string each supports.
cues.to-lab: Open Anatomy in Study Lab for the guitar you chose. Name the highlighted parts, then complete Part quiz, Name it fast and Part sprint. Get the part names right in the untimed quiz before using the timed games.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the guitar picture here. Say each part's name, then find it on the instrument if you have one. Don't make adjustments.
cues.in-lab: Say the name of each highlighted part, then find it on the guitar. Don't turn screws or make adjustments. Support the guitar securely before reaching for the screen. Finish the untimed part quiz before trying the timed games.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Complete Part quiz and get every part right. Name it fast and Part sprint are optional extra practice.
cues.success: Done. Next, holding the guitar and playing an open string.
cues.retry: If the nut and bridge are confused, trace one string. The nut is near the headstock. The bridge is on the body.
cues.wrap: Spend four minutes naming parts on the guitar. Trace the string from its tuning machine to the bridge. No metronome is needed. Next, work on holding the guitar.

lessons.title: Holding the guitar and first sound

cues.intro: In lesson four, you're going to support the guitar in a comfortable position and play ten clear open string notes.
cues.explain-a: Sit on a stable chair. Let your shoulders drop. Support the guitar so your fretting hand doesn't have to hold its weight. For a right handed setup, the body can rest on your right leg. A classical position on the left leg is another option. Reverse the setup if needed.
cues.explain-b: Let the neck angle slightly upwards. Keep the wrist comfortable, without a sharp bend. Use a strap for support while sitting or standing if needed. Glance at the side dots rather than tipping the whole guitar back. Keep breathing and moving normally.
cues.check: Relax both hands and check that the guitar remains supported. Adjust the body position or strap, then pluck an open string.
cues.to-lab: Open Mode Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode, guitar and Shape two. Select the first octave and both directions at sixty BPM. Keep scale playback stopped for the ten open string notes.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the lesson example on screen. Practise one short section without backing. Check the notes or counts before extending the section.
cues.in-lab: Play ten open notes with a pause after each. Listen for a clear start and a ringing note. Relax the shoulders between groups of notes. Keep the guitar supported and stop if the position or movement causes pain.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Mode Lab and tap Test me. Play the run once on your instrument. One correct run passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: An open note may rattle if another finger touches the vibrating string or the pluck is too large. Clear the string and reduce the picking movement.
cues.wrap: Spend three minutes on posture, including two minutes with the guitar supported. Play ten clear open notes at sixty BPM if comfortable. Stop for pain. Next, practise fretting.

cues.intro: Lesson five is about fretting clear notes with less pressure and practising the four finger exercise.
cues.explain-a: Your index finger is finger one. Middle is two, ring is three and fourth finger is four. Rest your thumb comfortably behind the neck. Curve a fingertip onto one string, just behind the fret wire on the headstock side. Don't press on the wire itself.
cues.explain-b: Reduce pressure until the note buzzes, then add only enough to clear it. For the warm up, place fingers one, two, three and four on neighbouring frets. This exercise doesn't change any Mode box fingering. Stop or use a labelled shift rather than forcing an index reach.
cues.check: Fret one note. Reduce pressure until it buzzes, then add only enough pressure to clear the sound.
cues.to-lab: Open Mode Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode, guitar and Shape two. Select the first octave and both directions at sixty BPM. Keep the scale fingering unchanged and playback stopped. Use one note per beat for the finger exercise.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the lesson example on screen. Practise one short section without backing. Check the notes or counts before extending the section.
cues.in-lab: Use one note per beat at sixty BPM across the strings. Keep the wrist comfortable and pressure light. If the first-position span strains the hand, stop and use a teacher-approved labelled shift. Don't change Mode box fingerings or force an index stretch.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Mode Lab and tap Test me. Play the run once on your instrument. One correct run passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: Buzzing often comes from pressing too far behind the wire. Move the fingertip closer before adding pressure. Reduce the exercise or use a labelled shift if the span strains the hand.
cues.wrap: Practise the four finger exercise for three minutes at sixty BPM, with rests. Aim for clear notes rather than speed. Don't force an index stretch. Next, practise picking.

cues.intro: In lesson six, you're going to alternate downstrokes and upstrokes on one open string, keeping the notes evenly spaced.
cues.explain-a: Hold the pick between your thumb and the side of your curled index finger. Leave a small tip showing, about two to three millimetres. Hold it securely without clenching. If it twists, make a small grip adjustment rather than tightening your whole arm.
cues.explain-b: A downstroke moves towards the floor. An upstroke returns. For this exercise, play down on a numbered beat and up on the word and. At sixty BPM, that gives you two notes per beat. Those half beat notes are called quavers.
cues.check: Mute one string lightly. Pick down, up, down, up. Check that both directions use a similar amount of movement.
cues.to-lab: Open Mode Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode, guitar and Shape two. Select the first octave, both directions, loop on and sixty BPM. Keep scale playback stopped for the open string picking exercise.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the lesson example on screen. Practise one short section without backing. Check the notes or counts before extending the section.
cues.in-lab: Use an open string and play two notes per beat at sixty BPM. Keep downstrokes and upstrokes similar in volume and spacing. Aim for four clear bars. Reduce picking depth if the string catches, and rest if the hand tightens or hurts.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Mode Lab and tap Test me. Play the run once on your instrument. One correct run passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: An upstroke can catch when too much pick passes through the string. Expose less tip and reduce the picking depth. Repeat one down and up pair slowly.
cues.wrap: Practise alternate picking for three minutes at sixty BPM. Play four bars of quavers, rest, then repeat. Check spacing and volume. Next, tune the strings.

cues.intro: In lesson seven, you're going to name the strings and tune them to standard pitch using small, careful adjustments.
cues.explain-a: From thickest to thinnest, the strings are low E, A, D, G, B and high e. The two E strings have the same letter name, but the high e sounds two octaves above the low E. Pluck just one string while the tuner listens.
cues.explain-b: Flat means too low. Sharp means too high. Check that the tuner shows the note you want before adjusting. Follow that string to its own tuning machine. Turn a small amount, pluck again and watch. Don't keep tightening if the pitch or string feels wrong. Ask for help if you're unsure.
cues.check: Find the G string and trace it to its tuning machine without turning it. Then check one open string with the tuner.
cues.to-lab: Open Mode Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode, guitar and Shape two. Keep both directions and sixty BPM selected, with playback stopped. Use the Study tuner to tune the open strings, not a scale note as a reference.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the tuner in this lesson. Pluck one open string, check its name and make small adjustments. Finish one string before moving to the next.
cues.in-lab: For an ear check, low E at fret five matches open A. A at five matches open D, and D at five matches open G. G at four matches open B. B at five matches high e. Begin with a reliable reference pitch.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Mode Lab and tap Test me. Play the run once on your instrument. One correct run passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: Other strings or a hard pluck can make the tuner reading unstable. Mute unused strings, pluck once and confirm the note you want before adjusting.
cues.wrap: Spend four minutes tuning carefully. Work towards all six strings within five cents in under two minutes. No tempo applies. Next, learn the musical alphabet.

cues.intro: In lesson eight, you're going to learn the musical alphabet and practise it forwards and backwards from different starting letters.
cues.explain-a: The musical letters are A, B, C, D, E, F and G. After G comes A again. Going backwards gives G, F, E, D, C, B and A. You can begin anywhere. From C, you get C, D, E, F, G, A, B and C.
cues.explain-b: The letters repeat in different pitch ranges. From one A up through the sequence to the next A is an octave. G up to the next A is only one step in the letter sequence, not an octave by itself. The fret distances between letters aren't all equal.
cues.check: Start at D and name the next four letters. Then start at C and move backwards through the sequence.
cues.to-lab: Open Fret Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode and guitar. Choose First four for the alphabet exercise in Practice. Read the exercise before playing. Use Practice before attempting the lesson check.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the fretboard picture here. Name the string, find the fret and check the note. Practise without playback before adding a timed exercise.
cues.in-lab: Name the note before selecting an answer. Restart from a known letter if the sequence is lost. Practise forwards and backwards. This naming exercise doesn't require fretting or a metronome, so rest the guitar while working through it.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Fret Lab and tap Test me. Play the answer once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the answer on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. Next, practise the alphabet from different starting letters.
cues.retry: If the sequence stops at G, practise G, A and B in isolation. Then place that group back into the full sequence.
cues.wrap: Spend three minutes reciting the alphabet forwards and backwards from different starting letters. Work without a metronome. Next, connect the note names to fret distances.

cues.intro: In lesson nine, you're going to connect sharps and flats with fret distances, using semitones and tones to work out note names.
cues.explain-a: One fret is one semitone. Moving towards the bridge by one fret raises the pitch by a semitone. Two frets make a tone. Between the natural notes B and C there's one semitone. There's also one semitone between E and F.
cues.explain-b: On the low E string, open E goes to F at fret one. F sharp is at fret two, and G at fret three. That fret two note can also be called G flat. On a normally fretted guitar, those names give the same pitch. The musical context helps choose the name.
cues.check: Play F at fret one on low E. Move up one fret and name the note as one semitone above F.
cues.to-lab: Open Fret Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode and guitar. Choose Semitone in Practice. Read the exercise before playing. Use Practice before attempting the lesson check.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the fretboard picture here. Name the string, find the fret and check the note. Practise without playback before adding a timed exercise.
cues.in-lab: Count fret distances rather than letters alone. Use B to C and E to F as one-fret checks. Keep the fingertip close behind the fret wire. Shift the hand when needed rather than holding one position and forcing a reach.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Fret Lab and tap Test me. Play the answer once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the answer on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: Counting two frets from E to F gives the wrong interval. Compare open E with fret one, then compare F at fret one with G at fret three.
cues.wrap: Spend four minutes finding semitones. Use sixty BPM only if it helps the playing. Next, memorise the open string names.

cues.intro: In lesson ten, you're going to name the six open strings in both directions and tell low E from high e.
cues.explain-a: An open string sounds without a fretting finger pressing it. From lowest to highest pitch, the standard guitar strings are low E, A, D, G, B and high e. The thickest is string six. The thinnest is string one.
cues.explain-b: The two E strings share a letter name, not the same pitch. Keep saying low E and high e when you need to tell them apart. In tab, high e is the top line. On your held guitar, low E is usually nearest your face. Check labels rather than relying on the picture's angle.
cues.check: Find A, B and D without playing. Pluck each one and say its name.
cues.to-lab: Open Fret Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode and guitar. Choose First four for the open string exercise in Practice. Read the exercise before playing. Use Practice before attempting the lesson check.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the fretboard picture here. Name the string, find the fret and check the note. Practise without playback before adding a timed exercise.
cues.in-lab: Play and name each open string, then point to the strings without labels. Build towards all six names in five seconds. Keep accuracy ahead of speed. Don't confuse string number one, high e, with string six, low E.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Fret Lab and tap Test me. Play the answer once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the answer on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. Next, name the six open strings without labels.
cues.retry: If B and high e are confused, find the thinnest string first. That's high e. The next thicker string is B. Add G after those are secure.
cues.wrap: Practise for three minutes. Name all six open strings in both directions and in a mixed order. Work towards five seconds without sacrificing accuracy. No metronome is needed.

cues.intro: In lesson eleven, you're going to read chord diagrams and use their markings to place your fingers and choose the first string to strum.
cues.explain-a: Imagine a guitar neck standing upright, facing you. The six vertical lines are strings. In this diagram, low E is on the left and high e is on the right. The horizontal lines mark frets. A thick line at the top marks the nut when it's shown.
cues.explain-b: A dot marks where a finger presses. Its number names the finger, not the fret. One is index, two is middle, three is ring and four is fourth finger. An open circle above a string means play it open. A cross means leave it out. A diagram higher on the neck uses a starting fret label.
cues.check: Check the D major diagram. Name the two silent strings and the string where the strum begins.
cues.to-lab: Open Chord Lab with C, Major family and Ionian mode. Select the first chord, C major, and the open position diagram. Compare the shape with the lesson illustration before placing the fingers.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the chord diagrams here. Name the starting fret, finger positions, open strings and silent strings before playing.
cues.in-lab: Read the diagram in this order: starting fret, finger positions, open strings and silent strings. Check ten diagrams. If playing, keep the fingertips curved, avoid touching neighbouring strings and stop for wrist pain. A finger number isn't a fret number.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Chord Lab and tap Test me. Play the chord once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the chord's notes instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: A number inside a dot names the finger, not the fret. Find the horizontal fret space first, then use the dot number to choose the finger.
cues.wrap: Spend four minutes reading ten diagrams. If playing them, use separate strums at sixty BPM. Check the starting string before each strum. Next, read single notes in tab.

cues.intro: This is lesson twelve. You're going to read single notes in tab and match each one to a string and fret.
cues.explain-a: Tab has six horizontal lines for a six string guitar. The top line is high e, the thinnest string. The bottom line is low E, the thickest. Check the string labels before reading the numbers.
cues.explain-b: A number tells you the fret on that string. Three on the A line means play fret three on the A string. Zero means play the string open. The number isn't a finger number. Read the line and number as a string and fret address.
cues.check: Name the string shown by the top tab line. Find fret three on the A string from its tab position.
cues.to-lab: Open Tab Lab with C, Major family and Ionian mode. Select four four time, treble clef and both notation and tab at seventy BPM. Open the exercise for this lesson before starting playback.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the tab example here. Read one position or rhythmic group at a time. Don't infer extra notes or missing rhythm from blank space.
cues.in-lab: Name the string first and fret second. Play one note, stop and compare it with the written position. Use the on screen fretboard before the real instrument if needed. Keep the guitar supported while changing between playing and screen controls.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Tab Lab and tap Start listening. Play the exercise once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes in order instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. Next, read ten single note positions.
cues.retry: A correct fret on the wrong string gives a different note. Trace the tab line to its label, name the string and then find the fret.
cues.wrap: Spend four minutes reading ten single note positions. Read without playback first. Use seventy BPM for the lab demonstration. Next, join positions into a melody.

cues.intro: In lesson thirteen, you're going to read notes from left to right and play a melody, starting with the five note example.
cues.explain-a: Read from left to right. Each new position tells you the next string and fret. The Study example starts with C at fret three on the A string. Then come open D, fret two on D, fret three on D and open G. You hear C, D, E, F and G.
cues.explain-b: Play the five notes separately before joining them. Move the hand naturally between positions. The lesson exercise in Tab Lab is an eight note melody. It goes up from C to G, then back down to C.
cues.check: Read the first two positions aloud, naming string and fret. Play those two notes before adding the next pair.
cues.to-lab: Open Tab Lab with C, Major family and Ionian mode. Select four four time, treble clef and both notation and tab at seventy BPM. Open the exercise for this lesson before starting playback.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the tab example here. Read one position or rhythmic group at a time. Don't infer extra notes or missing rhythm from blank space.
cues.in-lab: Read one note at a time and look only slightly ahead. The exercise opens at seventy BPM. Change it to sixty BPM before playback. Check for clear attacks and correct string changes.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Tab Lab and tap Start listening. Play the exercise once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes in order instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: Losing the position usually means reading too far ahead. Return to the last known note. Name the next string and fret, then practise that pair.
cues.wrap: Practise the eight note melody for five minutes at sixty BPM. Rest between repeats. Next, study pulse and tempo.

cues.intro: In lesson fourteen, you're going to follow a steady pulse at sixty BPM and keep it going for sixteen beats.
cues.explain-a: The pulse is the steady beat you can tap along with. Tempo is its speed. At sixty BPM, there is one beat each second. Changing tempo changes how fast the beat goes, not how many beats you count in a four beat bar.
cues.explain-b: Listen to four beats before joining in. Count one, two, three, four and repeat. Use four beats in each bar. A different first click marks the start of the bar. Maintain the same tapping pressure rather than striking harder on that click.
cues.check: Listen to four beats without tapping. Begin on the next beat one and continue for four bars.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock. Set sixty BPM, turn the practice click on and use a one bar count in. Tap sixteen steady beats.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the exercise here without backing. Count the full bar and practise the movement on muted strings or by tapping. Add pitched notes after the count is steady.
cues.in-lab: Tap sixteen beats at sixty BPM. During the timing game, continue the pulse when the click becomes silent. Use a relaxed tapping movement without hard strikes. Listen through the count in before starting, and don't chase a click after it has sounded.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Listen to four clicks, then tap the pulse. Keep tapping when the click goes quiet. Tap through to the end of the game.
cues.success: Done. Next, tap sixteen steady beats.
cues.retry: Reacting after each click produces late taps. Listen through a bar, prepare for the next beat and tap with it. Practise eight beats before extending to sixteen.
cues.wrap: Practise for three minutes at sixty BPM. Alternate one listening bar with one tapping bar, then tap sixteen beats continuously. Next, divide each beat into quavers.

cues.intro: In lesson fifteen, you're going to count four beats in a bar and divide each beat into two even halves.
cues.explain-a: In four four, count one, two, three, four. Each number is a beat. Now say one and two and three and four and. Keep the numbers at the same speed. The word and sits halfway between each pair of beats.
cues.explain-b: Those half beat notes are quavers. Two quavers fit into one crotchet beat here. Tap only the numbers first. Then add a light tap on every and. There should be eight evenly spaced taps in the bar, not a quick pair followed by a gap.
cues.check: Count one bar with the ands while tapping only the numbered beats. Check that each and falls halfway between two taps.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock. Begin at sixty BPM with the practice click on. Count quavers aloud, then use seventy BPM for the four bar goal.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the exercise here without backing. Count the full bar and practise the movement on muted strings or by tapping. Add pitched notes after the count is steady.
cues.in-lab: Begin at sixty BPM with the click. Keep the numbered beats steady while placing each and halfway between them. Work towards four bars aloud at seventy BPM. Practise voice and tapping without the guitar if the combined movements interrupt the count.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, count four bars of quavers aloud.
cues.retry: Rushed ands make the two halves uneven. Slow down, maintain the numbered beats and place each and halfway between them before increasing tempo.
cues.wrap: Practise counting for four minutes. Begin at sixty BPM and work towards four bars of quavers at seventy BPM. Next, apply the count to picking or strumming.

cues.intro: In lesson sixteen, you're going to play even quavers with a relaxed hand movement, using strums on guitar or single string plucks on bass.
cues.explain-a: For guitar, rest the fretting fingers lightly across the strings to mute them. Strum down on the numbers and up on the ands. Keep the shoulder relaxed. Allow the wrist and forearm to move without locking either joint.
cues.explain-b: For bass, keep the same spoken count and alternate comfortable plucking fingers on one muted string. The goal is an even quaver rhythm, not a particular guitar strumming motion. Listen for equal spacing and a light, controlled sound.
cues.check: Make the movement silently for one bar. Then contact the muted string or strings on each count without changing the spacing.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock at seventy BPM. Use muted guitar strums or the bass plucking exercise for the instrument you chose.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the exercise here without backing. Count the full bar and practise the movement on muted strings or by tapping. Add pitched notes after the count is steady.
cues.in-lab: Aim for four bars of even quavers at seventy BPM. On guitar, continue the down and up movement through strokes that miss the strings. On bass, alternate plucks on one muted string. Keep the shoulder relaxed and stop for pain, tingling or strain.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Use the rhythm game for the instrument you chose. Follow the guitar strums or bass plucking exercise after the count in. Play through to the end of the game.
cues.success: Done. Next, check four bars of the muted string exercise.
cues.retry: Tension can make the movement uneven. Stop, release the shoulder and reduce the movement. Practise one beat before adding the rest of the bar.
cues.wrap: Practise for three minutes at seventy BPM, or slower while learning. Aim for four even bars with rests between attempts. Use the exercise for the instrument you chose.

cues.intro: In lesson seventeen, you're going to build eight open chords and check which strings should ring before you strum.
cues.explain-a: Start with E minor. Put finger two on the A string at fret two and finger three on the D string at fret two. Leave the other strings open and strum all six. Add finger one on the G string at fret one to hear E major.
cues.explain-b: Follow the diagrams for A minor, A major, D major, D minor, G major and C major. A, A minor and C begin on the A string. D and D minor begin on the D string. Keep neighbouring fingertips clear of the open strings.
cues.check: Pick the six E minor strings separately. Compare E minor with E major, adding finger one on G at fret one.
cues.to-lab: Open Chord Lab with C, Major family and Ionian mode. Select the first chord, C major, and the open position diagram. Compare the shape with the lesson illustration before placing the fingers.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the open chord diagrams here. Build one shape and check each intended string before strumming. Leave out the strings marked with a cross.
cues.in-lab: Check every intended string before four strums on each chord. State the chord name before playing. Divide the eight shapes across short sessions. Rebuild a crowded shape slowly and use only enough pressure for a clear sound. Stop for pain.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Chord Lab and tap Test me. Play the chord once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the chord's notes instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: A flat finger may silence a neighbouring string. Find the muted string with separate plucks. Curve the finger touching it and move it closer behind its fret.
cues.wrap: Spend five minutes on two open chords at sixty BPM. Work towards four clear strums on each of all eight chords over several sessions. Next, examine open C in detail.

cues.intro: In lesson eighteen, you're going to play open C major with five clear strings, then practise changing between C and A minor.
cues.explain-a: Place finger three on A at fret three, finger two on D at fret two and finger one on B at fret one. Leave G and high e open. Strum from A and keep low E silent.
cues.explain-b: The cross above low E means leave that string out. The circles above G and high e mean play them open. From A across, the sounding notes are C, E, G, C and E. Five strings sound, using the three chord notes C, E and G.
cues.check: Pick the G string on its own. If it's dull, check whether the second finger is touching it. Repeat this check on each of the five strings.
cues.to-lab: Open Chord Lab in C, with Major family and Ionian mode. Select the first chord, C major, and its open position diagram. Match the diagram to the lesson before playing. Use open C, not a different C voicing.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the open C diagram here. Place the three fingers and leave G and high e open. Pick each of the five sounding strings on its own. Strum from A and leave low E silent.
cues.in-lab: Keep the fingers curved. Finger three must leave D clear, and finger two must leave G clear. Play four bars with one strum per beat at sixty BPM. Rest between attempts. Stop and ask for help if the reach causes pain.
cues.back: Check that all five strings ring and low E remains silent. Repeat any unclear string before testing the C to A minor change.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, repeat the C to A minor change at sixty BPM.
cues.retry: A dull string is often touched by a neighbouring finger. Pick each string to find the problem. Move the finger that's touching it out of the way and check again. Don't press harder across the whole chord.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes at sixty BPM. Check all five strings three times, then change between C and A minor. Keep fingers one and two down. Move finger three to G at fret two. Aim for eight clean changes in thirty seconds.

cues.intro: This is lesson nineteen. You're going to play strumming patterns while keeping an even down and up movement through the silent strokes.
cues.explain-a: Start with downstrokes on one, two, three and four. Let the hand return on each and, even when it misses the strings. Then try down, down up, down, down up. The sounding counts are one, two and, three, four and.
cues.explain-b: The folk pattern sounds on one, two, the and after two, the and after three, four and the and after four. Your hand passes the strings silently on beat three. Keep counting the full bar, including the counts where you don't play.
cues.check: Clap the sounding counts while saying every count aloud. Keep beat three in the count even when the strumming hand misses the strings.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with G, Major family, Ionian mode and folk at seventy BPM. Select a four bar backing length and repeat the pattern for eight bars.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the exercise here without backing. Count the full bar and practise the movement on muted strings or by tapping. Add pitched notes after the count is steady.
cues.in-lab: Use muted strings or an open chord that matches the backing. Maintain even gaps for eight bars at seventy BPM. The backing is in G major; follow its displayed chord changes. Keep the wrist relaxed and practise one pattern before changing it.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, play the pattern for eight bars.
cues.retry: Stopping at a silent stroke disrupts the rhythm. Return to continuous down and up movement, then let one stroke pass the strings without contact.
cues.wrap: Practise one pattern for five minutes at seventy BPM, or slower initially. Aim for eight steady bars. Use muted strings or follow the backing chords. Next, practise chord changes.

cues.intro: In lesson twenty, you're going to change between A minor and C using shared finger positions, then count clear changes over one minute.
cues.explain-a: Begin with A minor and C. Finger one stays on B at fret one. Finger two stays on D at fret two. Finger three moves between G at fret two for A minor and A at fret three for C. Keep the two shared fingers in place without clamping them down.
cues.explain-b: First make the movement silently. Then strum once after each clean landing. Count only changes that sound clear. Aim for thirty clean changes in one minute. Don't increase speed until both shapes are clear.
cues.check: Move between A minor and C without strumming. Keep finger one on B at fret one and finger two on D at fret two.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock. Select sixty BPM and two chords. Read the chord names before playing. Practise A minor and C without backing if those aren't the two chords shown.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the exercise here without backing. Count the full bar and practise the movement on muted strings or by tapping. Add pitched notes after the count is steady.
cues.in-lab: Use sixty BPM. Match the two played chords to the backing. Practise A minor and C without backing if those aren't the chords shown. Keep fingers near the strings, release excess pressure during movement and count only clear changes in the one minute exercise.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Play the strumming timing game through to the end. Then count your clear chord changes over one minute.
cues.success: Done. Next, count clear chord changes for one minute.
cues.retry: Lifting all fingers makes this change unnecessarily large. Keep the two shared fingers down and practise moving only finger three. Add a strum after each clear landing.
cues.wrap: Practise one pair for five minutes at sixty BPM. Count clean changes for one minute after warming up. Work towards thirty per minute. Next, practise rests and muted chucks.

cues.intro: In lesson twenty one, you're going to stop a ringing chord for a rest and make a muted chuck sound.
cues.explain-a: When you miss the strings, the previous chord may keep ringing. For a true rest, stop that sound lightly. Use a light touch from the picking hand or carefully release the fretting pressure. Open strings need a muting touch too. If you lift every finger away, open strings may keep ringing. Give them a light muting touch too.
cues.explain-b: A chuck is a short, percussive strum. Lightly touch the strings so they don't ring as clear pitches, then brush across them. Keep the pressure light enough not to fret a new note. put that dry sound on beats two and four.
cues.check: Strum a chord and let it ring. Repeat it, then stop the sound on the next count. Compare a missed stroke with actual silence.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with G, Major family, Ionian mode and reggae at seventy BPM. Play four bars with chucks on beats two and four.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the exercise here without backing. Count the full bar and practise the movement on muted strings or by tapping. Add pitched notes after the count is steady.
cues.in-lab: Count four bars and place chucks on beats two and four. Start with all strings muted. Listen for a short percussive sound without pitched open strings underneath. Brush the strings lightly. A missed stroke can leave a chord ringing; a rest must stop it.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: A ringing chuck means some strings aren't muted. Touch the open strings lightly as well as releasing fretting pressure, then test a short strum.
cues.wrap: Practise for four minutes at seventy BPM. Alternate ringing sounds with silence and place chucks on beats two and four for four bars. Next, read chord columns in tab.

cues.intro: In lesson twenty two, you're going to read chords in tab and play the stacked notes at the same time.
cues.explain-a: Numbers directly above one another form a column. Play those positions at once rather than reading down the column as a melody. E minor has open low E, fret two on A, fret two on D, then open G, B and high e.
cues.explain-b: Compare C major. Leave low E out, then play A at fret three, D at fret two, open G, B at fret one and open high e. In a chord shape, a cross can mean leave that string out. In rhythmic tab, crosses can ask for muted percussive notes. Check how the marking is used.
cues.check: Name the six sounding strings in the E minor column. Then name where the C major strum begins.
cues.to-lab: Open Tab Lab with C, Major family and Ionian mode. Select four four time, treble clef and both notation and tab at seventy BPM. Open the exercise for this lesson before starting playback.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the tab example here. Read one position or rhythmic group at a time. Don't infer extra notes or missing rhythm from blank space.
cues.in-lab: Read the whole chord column before playing. Check the shape by picking each string, then strum. Work through four bars and leave low E out of the C chord. Keep the wrist comfortable. Stop if the shape causes pain rather than pressing harder.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Tab Lab and tap Start listening. Play the exercise once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes in order instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. Next, play the four chord tab bars.
cues.retry: Reading down a chord column as a melody changes the instruction. Read the whole stack before playing, then strum the strings that should sound once.
cues.wrap: Practise the four chord tab bars for five minutes. Begin at sixty BPM if needed, then use seventy BPM. Check which strings are left out of each chord. Next, read note lengths.

cues.intro: In lesson twenty three, you're going to read note lengths and rests, then play the written rhythm rather than guess from tab spacing.
cues.explain-a: Plain text tab may not show exact timing. In combined notation and tab, the staff or rhythmic stems show note lengths. The tab gives the string and fret. Read the time signature too. Today's four four bars hold four crotchet beats each.
cues.explain-b: In the Study example, a crotchet lasts one beat, two quavers share the next beat and a minim lasts two beats. Count the full bar before you play. A note held for two beats doesn't need a second attack just because the next click arrives.
cues.check: Clap the rhythm without fretting. Name the note that lasts two beats and continue counting through its full length.
cues.to-lab: Open Tab Lab with C, Major family and Ionian mode. Select four four time, treble clef and both notation and tab at seventy BPM. Open the exercise for this lesson before starting playback.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the tab example here. Read one position or rhythmic group at a time. Don't infer extra notes or missing rhythm from blank space.
cues.in-lab: Loop the four bar riff at seventy BPM. Check note endings as well as attacks. Hold each note for its written value and mute at rests. Practise the rhythm without fretting first if finding the notes prevents accurate counting.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Tab Lab and tap Start listening. Play the exercise once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes in order instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: A held note ending early shortens the bar. Count its full written value aloud while it rings. Practise that bar before joining it to the next.
cues.wrap: Practise the four bar rhythmic riff for five minutes at seventy BPM, or slower initially. Check held notes and rests as well as attacks. Next, name technique symbols.

cues.intro: In lesson twenty four, you're going to learn what the main tab technique symbols mean before trying the movements they describe.
cues.explain-a: The letter h between frets means hammer on. Pick the first note, then place another finger firmly enough to sound the next. The letter p means pull off. Hold the lower note first, then release the higher finger with a small controlled motion to sound it.
cues.explain-b: A rising slash means slide up, and a falling slash means slide down. The letter b can mark a bend towards a pitch to aim for. A wavy line means vibrato. The letters P M mark palm muting. Crosses in a rhythmic note position can mark dead, percussive notes.
cues.check: Name the action shown by each symbol. State that a slide moves along the string, while a bend changes pitch by moving the string across the fretboard.
cues.to-lab: Open Tab Lab with C, Major family and Ionian mode. Select four four time, treble clef and both notation and tab at seventy BPM. Open the exercise for this lesson before starting playback.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the tab example here. Read one position or rhythmic group at a time. Don't infer extra notes or missing rhythm from blank space.
cues.in-lab: Name ten symbols before physically attempting them. In a bend, the arrow and the word full mean raise the pitch by one whole tone. Don't press another fret. Listen to the demonstration instead of forcing a bend or wide reach. Stop for pain or strain.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Tab Lab and tap Start listening. Play the exercise once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes in order instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. Next, read the riff.
cues.retry: Hammer ons and pull offs use different actions. For a hammer on, add the higher finger. For a pull off, hold the lower note before releasing the higher finger.
cues.wrap: Spend four minutes naming ten symbols. Use the seventy BPM demonstration or name them without playback. Don't force bends or wide reaches. Next, read a riff.

cues.intro: In lesson twenty five, you're going to learn a riff in short groups, then join the notes and check the rhythm.
cues.explain-a: The Study riff uses open low E, fret three on low E, open A, fret two on A, open D, fret two on D, fret two on A and open A. Read that slowly from left to right. These notes come from the E minor pentatonic collection.
cues.explain-b: Learn the notes in groups of two, then join the groups. Begin at seventy BPM. The playing goal is four bars at eighty BPM, so increase tempo only after the notes and rhythm are accurate. Use the written exercise for the four bar rhythm.
cues.check: Read the first four positions aloud, including string names. Play them without backing before attempting the full phrase.
cues.to-lab: Open Tab Lab with C, Major family and Ionian mode. Select four four time, treble clef and both notation and tab at seventy BPM. Open the exercise for this lesson before starting playback.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the tab example here. Read one position or rhythmic group at a time. Don't infer extra notes or missing rhythm from blank space.
cues.in-lab: Keep picking movements small and fretting fingers near the strings. Check even spacing and clear string changes. Use the written four bar exercise to check the full phrase. The eight note example alone doesn't show four bars of rhythm. Rest between repeats.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Tab Lab and tap Start listening. Play the exercise once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes in order instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: A missed string crossing needs isolated practice. Repeat the note before the crossing and the note after it slowly, then rejoin the phrase.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes, starting at seventy BPM and working towards eighty. Use the written four bar exercise for that goal. The eight note example can be learned without assigning it a four bar rhythm.

cues.intro: This is lesson twenty six. You're going to build power chords and move the same shape between different roots without stretching your index finger.
cues.explain-a: A power chord uses a root and a perfect fifth. You can add another root an octave higher. Because it has no third, the shape alone is neither major nor minor. G five means a G power chord, not five different notes.
cues.explain-b: For G five, put finger one on low E at fret three and finger three on A at fret five. Finger four can add D at fret five for the octave. Keep the spare strings quiet. Move the whole shape for A five at fret five, C five at fret eight and D five at fret ten.
cues.check: Play the two note G power chord. Name G under finger one, then shift the whole shape to the A position.
cues.to-lab: Open Chord Lab with C, Major family and Ionian mode. It opens on C five in Power voicing. Tap the G five, A five, C five and D five chips to see each shape. Work towards moving through the four roots at eighty BPM.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the power chord diagrams here. Start with the two note G shape, then move the whole hand to A. Keep spare strings silent.
cues.in-lab: Place each shape before trying to move at eighty BPM. Strum only the strings that should sound and lightly mute the others. Move the whole hand between roots. If the span strains the hand, stop and ask for a comfortable way to play it. Don't force an index stretch.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Chord Lab and tap Test me. Play the chord once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the chord's notes instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: Spare strings can hide the power chord. Pick only the strings that should sound and lightly mute the others. Check each note you want before strumming again.
cues.wrap: Practise G five, A five, C five and D five for four minutes. Work towards eighty BPM, resting between attempts. Shift the whole hand without an index stretch. Next, practise full chord progressions.

cues.intro: In lesson twenty seven, you're going to play G, C, D and G as a four bar progression, then repeat it for eight bars.
cues.explain-a: In G major, G is chord one, C is chord four and D is chord five. The numbers name their places in the key. Name the chords and compare the return from D to G.
cues.explain-b: Play one bar on each chord, with four light downstrums in the bar. That makes a four bar progression. Repeat it once for eight bars. Check the starting string for each shape. G uses all six strings, C starts on A and D starts on D.
cues.check: Build G, C and D without strumming. Name the starting string for each chord and use the shortest required strum on D.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock. Select seventy BPM, four chords and triad voicings. Check that the progression is G, C, D and G. Otherwise, practise that progression without backing.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the exercise here without backing. Count the full bar and practise the movement on muted strings or by tapping. Add pitched notes after the count is steady.
cues.in-lab: Count through the changes at seventy BPM. If a grip is late, maintain the count and resume on a clear beat. Practise that change on its own after that. Check the starting string on each chord and stop for pain or strain.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: A muddy D chord often includes low E or A. Begin on the open D string and reduce the stroke width before returning to the progression.
cues.wrap: Practise G, C, D and G for five minutes at seventy BPM. Aim for eight steady bars, with four downstrums per bar. Next, use fret markers to find notes.

cues.intro: In lesson twenty eight, you're going to use fret markers to find notes without counting every fret from the nut.
cues.explain-a: Many guitars mark frets three, five, seven, nine and twelve. Fret twelve often has a double marker. Your guitar may use a different design, so check the fret numbers rather than assuming every decoration follows this pattern.
cues.explain-b: On low E, those frets sound G, A, B, C sharp and E. On A, they sound C, D, E, F sharp and A. Notice that the fret nine notes are sharp here. A marker shows a position, not a promise that its note belongs to C major.
cues.check: Find fret five using a side marker. Name the note on low E, then name the note at the same fret on A.
cues.to-lab: Open Fret Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode and guitar. Choose Landmarks in Practice. Read the exercise before playing. Use Practice before attempting the lesson check.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the fretboard picture here. Name the string, find the fret and check the note. Practise without playback before adding a timed exercise.
cues.in-lab: Find the marker, then check the fret and string. Get the landmark answers right before you go faster. Shift the hand towards each position rather than reaching from a fixed point. Marker designs vary between instruments.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Fret Lab and tap Test me. Play the answer once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the answer on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: A correct fret on a different string has a different note name. At fret five, low E gives A and the A string gives D. Name both string and fret.
cues.wrap: Practise markers and their notes for four minutes without a metronome. Get the landmark answers right before you go faster. Next, find natural notes on low E and A.

cues.intro: In lesson twenty nine, you're going to find natural notes on low E and A using open strings, fret markers and semitone pairs.
cues.explain-a: On low E, the natural notes are open E, F at fret one, G at three, A at five, B at seven, C at eight, D at ten and E at twelve. B to C and E to F stay one fret apart.
cues.explain-b: On A, start with open A. B is at fret two, C at three, D at five, E at seven, F at eight, G at ten and A at twelve. Learn a few at a time. Use a nearby note you know instead of recounting the whole string every time.
cues.check: Find C on A, then C on low E. Name both fret numbers and find the B immediately below each C.
cues.to-lab: Open Fret Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode and guitar. Choose Multi for the natural note exercise in Practice. Read the exercise before playing. Use Practice before attempting the lesson check.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the fretboard picture here. Name the string, find the fret and check the note. Practise without playback before adding a timed exercise.
cues.in-lab: Name the string before finding the note. Begin without a timer, then find the notes faster. This is a note naming goal, not a playing speed drill. Move between positions comfortably and use light fingertip pressure.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Fret Lab and tap Test me. Play the answer once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the answer on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: Guessing fret distances can give the wrong note. Start from the nearest note you know and count semitones. Remember that B to C and E to F are one fret apart.
cues.wrap: Practise natural notes for five minutes. Find them faster without rushing your playing movements. No playing tempo is required. Next, find octaves.

cues.intro: In lesson thirty, you're going to find octave pairs across the neck and check how the string pair changes the fret spacing.
cues.explain-a: Play G on low E at fret three, then G on D at fret five. This moves two strings towards the thinner strings and two frets towards the bridge. The same shape works from A to G: C on A at fret three gives C an octave higher on G at fret five.
cues.explain-b: That two fret rule isn't universal on guitar. From D to B, or G to high e, move two strings and three frets. The tuning gap between G and B changes the shape. Also, the same pitch in two places is a unison, not an octave.
cues.check: Play G on low E at fret three, then G on D at fret five. Compare how high or low they sound. Both have the note name G.
cues.to-lab: Open Fret Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode and guitar. Choose Multi for the octave exercise in Practice. Read the exercise before playing. Use Practice before attempting the lesson check.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the fretboard picture here. Name the string, find the fret and check the note. Practise without playback before adding a timed exercise.
cues.in-lab: Release the lower note before finding its octave if holding both positions causes strain. Shift the whole hand as needed. Compare the note names and how high or low they sound. Check the string pair before using either the two-fret or three-fret offset.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Fret Lab and tap Test me. Play the answer once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the answer on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. Next, practise the octave pairs on the guitar.
cues.retry: An incorrect octave often comes from using the wrong fret offset. Check the string pair. Start with low E at three and D at five before trying another pair.
cues.wrap: Practise octave pairs for four minutes. Use sixty BPM if useful. Release between notes rather than forcing a reach. Next, organise practice sessions.

cues.intro: In lesson thirty one, you're going to plan one focused practice task and keep a record of five short sessions across several days.
cues.explain-a: Check tuning and posture, then warm up with an easy exercise. Choose one specific skill, such as a clear C chord or a short note pattern. State the result to check before starting the practice timer.
cues.explain-b: Use a tempo that allows accurate repetitions. Increase it by a small amount only after several clear attempts. Record the task, tempo and one observation. Complete five recorded sessions across several days, not five repetitions within one session.
cues.check: Choose one task and state its result clearly. For open C, use five clear strings on three consecutive checks.
cues.to-lab: Open Mode Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode, guitar and Shape two. Select both directions, loop on and sixty BPM. Practise the chosen short task, then record the task, tempo and one observation.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the written practice plan here. Choose one task, practise for a few minutes and record the task, tempo and one observation.
cues.in-lab: Use sixty BPM for a suitable note exercise and rest between attempts. Keep Mode fingerings unchanged. Select a short section if the full scale exceeds the current playing ability. Stop for pain, numbness or persistent tension. Record the task, tempo and one observation.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Open Mode Lab and tap Test me. Play the run once on your instrument. One correct run passes the check. With no mic, tap the notes on the neck instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. Next, add an entry to the five session practice log.
cues.retry: An unfocused session needs a smaller task. Stop the loop, choose one result and write it down. Make a short attempt and record what changed.
cues.wrap: Practise the chosen task for five minutes at sixty BPM if it uses a beat. Record the task, tempo and one observation. Repeat on four more days. Next, study the amplifier signal path.

cues.intro: In lesson thirty two, you're going to follow the signal from guitar to amplifier and speaker, and check the connections with the volume down.
cues.explain-a: For a basic setup, the guitar output connects to the amplifier input with an instrument cable. The amplifier drives its speaker. Turn volume down before connecting or disconnecting. Use dry hands and undamaged equipment. Don't open an amplifier or touch anything inside it.
cues.explain-b: Gain controls how strongly a stage is driven and may add distortion. Master volume usually controls the final level, though amplifiers vary. Start low, play a note and raise the level gradually. A speaker output isn't an instrument input. Tube amplifiers need the correct speaker load; follow the maker's instructions.
cues.check: With volume down, find the guitar output and amplifier instrument input. Trace the connection without changing any unfamiliar control.
cues.to-lab: Stay in Study Lab. Trace the signal path on the picture. Keep amplifier volume down while checking the connections. Raise it gradually only after you've checked them.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the signal path picture here. Trace the cable connections without changing unfamiliar controls. Keep amplifier volume down.
cues.in-lab: Check cable seating, guitar volume and the correct input before raising amplifier volume. Use comfortable listening levels. Don't test unfamiliar speaker connections by trial and error. Ask a teacher or technician, and stop using damaged cables, sockets or power leads.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, compare pickup sounds.
cues.retry: No sound may come from a cable or input problem. Turn down, check the connection and test a known working instrument cable. Don't compensate with maximum gain.
cues.wrap: Spend four minutes following the signal path. Practise the connection routine with volume down. Don't open equipment or use damaged leads. No tempo applies. Next, compare pickups.

cues.intro: This is lesson thirty three. You're going to compare pickup positions using the same phrase, so you can hear what each position changes.
cues.explain-a: A magnetic pickup senses the movement of suitable metal strings. Many guitars use single coil pickups, humbuckers or a mixture. A humbucker uses two coils arranged to reduce common electrical hum. That doesn't make it silent in every situation, and pickup designs vary.
cues.explain-b: The bridge pickup often sounds brighter and more focused. A neck pickup often sounds rounder. The selector chooses pickups or combinations. These are starting points for listening, not rules about which one you must use for a style. Your hands and amp settings matter too.
cues.check: Play the same phrase in two selector positions. Describe the change in brightness and attack without changing the amplifier controls.
cues.to-lab: Stay in Study Lab. Compare the pickup pictures and sounds. On an electric guitar, use the same phrase in two selector positions at a comfortable volume.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the pickup illustration here. Find the selector if the instrument has one. Return to the labelled sound comparison before taking the listening or naming check.
cues.in-lab: Use the same phrase and amplifier settings for each comparison. Keep listening volume comfortable and support the instrument while moving the selector. If the instrument has no pickups, use the labelled examples. Compare the two end positions before intermediate combinations.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, compare guitar effects.
cues.retry: Small differences are harder to hear through effects. Use a clean sound and compare the two end positions first, using one held note and then one short chord.
cues.wrap: Compare pickup positions for four minutes. Use a short phrase at sixty BPM if useful and keep other settings unchanged. Next, compare effect families.

cues.intro: In lesson thirty four, you're going to compare drive, delay, reverb and modulation with a dry guitar sound, one effect at a time.
cues.explain-a: Drive adds grit or distortion. Delay repeats the sound after a short gap. Reverb suggests a space around it. Modulation effects, such as chorus or tremolo, change some part of the sound over time. Chorus and tremolo aren't the same effect, even though both can create movement.
cues.explain-b: A useful starting order is guitar, drive, modulation, delay, reverb, then amplifier input. Other orders can sound good too. Some effects work well in an amplifier's effects loop, if the equipment supports it. Check the manual rather than plugging into unfamiliar sockets.
cues.check: Listen to the dry phrase and one effect. Choose whether the change adds distortion, repeats, space or modulation.
cues.to-lab: Stay in Study Lab. Listen to the dry guitar phrase and one effect. Name the audible change before adding another effect. Keep listening volume comfortable.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Review the effect descriptions here. Name distortion, repeats, space and modulation from known sounds. Return to the labelled comparison before taking the listening or naming check.
cues.in-lab: Use the same phrase and listening volume for each comparison. Add one effect before combining two. Turn down before changing connections. Use only the power supply type and voltage stated by the maker. Stop if equipment is damaged or behaves unexpectedly. Compare each change with the dry sound.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, change tone with your picking touch.
cues.retry: Too many effects can hide the original phrase. Switch them off, then add one at a low mix level. Reduce repeats before adding another effect.
cues.wrap: Compare dry sound with one effect at a time for five minutes. Use a phrase at sixty BPM if useful. Keep volume comfortable and use the power supply type and voltage the maker states. Next, shape tone with picking touch.

cues.intro: In lesson thirty five, you're going to change tone with your picking touch and one equipment control, comparing the same phrase each time.
cues.explain-a: Play the same note lightly and then more firmly. Notice the change in attack and level. Try picking a small nearer the neck, then nearer the bridge. Stay clear of any sharp hardware. The position changes the balance of the sound even before an effect is added.
cues.explain-b: Change one equipment control, such as the guitar tone knob or one amplifier tone control. Repeat the same phrase for comparison. A sound that works alone may not suit a full band, so judge the tone in its musical context.
cues.check: Play a short phrase with two different picking touches. Compare the attack and tone before changing any equipment control.
cues.to-lab: Stay in Study Lab. Compare the same phrase with different picking touches, then change one tone control. Check which change caused each sound difference.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Compare two picking touches on the same note without changing controls. Listen for the change in attack and tone before adjusting equipment.
cues.in-lab: Keep both comparisons at comfortable volume. Vary picking touch without striking harder than is comfortable. Listen for clear attacks and controlled string noise. Record one equipment setting and one picking choice. Change only one thing before repeating the same phrase.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: Changing several controls prevents a clear comparison. Return to a clean starting sound, change one control and play the same phrase again.
cues.wrap: Explore touch for five minutes at sixty BPM, then change one tone control. Record one setting and one picking choice that suit the phrase. Next, check instrument care and setup issues.

cues.intro: In lesson thirty six, you're going to check the guitar for care and setup issues and learn which jobs need a teacher or technician.
cues.explain-a: Wipe the strings and instrument with an appropriate soft cloth after playing. Keep liquids away from electronics and follow the maker's care guidance for your finish. Check for loose or damaged parts without taking anything apart. Store the guitar securely, away from heat and sudden climate changes.
cues.explain-b: Action means string height above the frets. Intonation is how well fretted pitches agree across the neck. A guitar can have its open strings in tune while a fretted note sounds wrong. String gauge, setup and excess finger pressure can all affect the result.
cues.check: Play an open string and one lightly fretted note. Note any buzz or unusual resistance without adjusting the instrument.
cues.to-lab: Stay in Study Lab. Follow the care steps and check the instrument without unfamiliar adjustments. Record any issue that needs a teacher or technician.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Check the instrument without adjustments. Record any care or setup issue for a teacher or technician. Leave repairs and unfamiliar controls alone.
cues.in-lab: Follow the care instructions or demonstration. Use a teacher or reliable instrument-specific guide for a first string change. Watch sharp string ends and avoid overtightening. Leave unfamiliar truss rod, bridge and electrical repairs to a qualified person. Don't adjust a problem that hasn't been checked.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, plan a session across the labs.
cues.retry: A high fretted note may sound sharp from excess pressure or setup. Retune the open string and reduce finger pressure. If the issue remains, record the fret and request a setup check.
cues.wrap: Spend four minutes checking and wiping down the guitar. Record any issue for a teacher or technician. Make no unfamiliar adjustments. No tempo applies. Next, combine the practice labs.

lessons.title: Bridge to Notation & Harmony: your first hour in the Labs

cues.intro: In lesson thirty seven, you're going to work through six practice parts across Mode, Fret, Jam, Chord, Tab and Songwriter, keeping a short record of each.
cues.explain-a: Spend about ten minutes on each part, including a short rest and a practice note. In Mode, use C Ionian, Shape two, both directions over two octaves at sixty BPM. Listen first, then play a short comfortable section before trying the full range.
