cues.explain-b: Find C notes in Fret, keep a pulse in Jam, check open C in Chord, read a phrase in Tab and record an idea in Songwriter. Follow the practice cards chosen by the teacher. Complete and review one task before starting the next.
cues.check: Read the first practice card. State its task and the result to check before beginning. Pause between parts when needed.
cues.to-lab: Begin in Mode Lab with C, Major family, Ionian mode, guitar and Shape two. Select both directions over two octaves at sixty BPM. Follow the practice cards through the six labs. Use Next part after finishing the task on each card.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Complete one previously learned task and record the work. Use a short chord, note finding or pulse exercise. Resume the remaining practice cards on another day.
cues.in-lab: Keep each task within a comfortable playing range. Listen before attempting a full two octave scale and leave Mode fingerings unchanged. Stop for pain and include rests. Record the work actually practised and one observation before moving to the next part.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, continue to reading on guitar or groove studies on bass.
cues.retry: A full hour may be too long for one session. Complete one ten minute part, including its rest, and record the stopping point. Resume with the next part on another day.
cues.wrap: Complete six ten minute parts over one or more days. Use sixty BPM where shown and include rests. Record what was practised. Guitar continues to reading; bass continues to groove studies.

cues.intro: In lesson thirty eight, you're going to play bass roots with the drums and control when each note starts and stops.
cues.explain-a: The bass links rhythm and harmony. The kick drum gives a useful timing reference. The chord's root tells you its name. For a G chord, the root is G. On a standard four string bass, find G on the E string at fret three.
cues.explain-b: Play G once per beat and listen to its length. Check both when the note starts and when it stops against the rhythm. Touch or release the string lightly to leave a clear gap. Leave some spaces without adding notes.
cues.check: Listen through one drum bar. Pick out the low kick sound, then place a G root on a clear beat.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with bass, G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock at seventy BPM. Mute the backing bass. Read the chord names before starting and play the lesson exercise for eight bars.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the bass example here without backing. Find the notes, mute spare strings and practise the phrase slowly. Add drums after the note order is secure.
cues.in-lab: Follow the roots shown when chords change. Play eight bars at seventy BPM with the backing bass muted. Check note lengths and clear endings as well as attacks. Use light plucking, support the instrument and stop for pain or tingling.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: A late note may come from reacting after the drum attack. Listen through a bar first, then prepare for one beat and place a single root with it.
cues.wrap: Practise roots for five minutes at seventy BPM. Play eight bars, rest and check timing and note endings. Keep the backing bass muted. Next, follow chord changes.

cues.intro: In lesson thirty nine, you're going to follow chord changes with matching bass roots and prepare each new note before the change.
cues.explain-a: A chord's root is the note it's named after. For G, C, D and back to G, the bass roots are G, C, D and G. On bass, play G on E at fret three, C on A at fret three and D on A at fret five.
cues.explain-b: Find the positions without the track first. Read the chord names and prepare the next root before the change. Follow the chord order on screen. A generated backing may use a different order from the G, C, D and G example.
cues.check: Find G, C and D in order. Practise the move from C to D on the A string before starting the backing.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with bass, G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock at seventy BPM. Mute the backing bass. Read the chord names before starting and play the lesson exercise for eight bars.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the bass example here without backing. Find the notes, mute spare strings and practise the phrase slowly. Add drums after the note order is secure.
cues.in-lab: Follow chord changes for eight bars at seventy BPM. Mute the backing bass before starting. Control note lengths and spare strings. Move the whole hand towards each position rather than forcing a fixed reach. Prepare the next root before the chord changes.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: Staying on the previous root means the next chord was not prepared. Stop playback, name the chord order and practise one root at each change.
cues.wrap: Practise following roots for five minutes at seventy BPM. Aim for eight bars with clean changes and the backing bass muted. Next, add the fifth.

cues.intro: This is lesson forty. You're going to alternate a bass root and its fifth, beginning with G and D.
cues.explain-a: Start with G on the E string at fret three. Its perfect fifth above is D on the A string at fret five. From this root string, the fifth is one string towards the thinner strings and two frets towards the bridge. This example fits standard four string bass tuning.
cues.explain-b: Alternate G, D, G and D, one note per beat. Say root, fifth, root, fifth as you play. When the chord changes, the pair must move to fit the new root. The teaching pair is for G; don't keep playing it over every possible chord.
cues.check: Play G followed by D. Name G as the root and D as its fifth, then repeat the pair.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with bass, G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock at seventy BPM. Mute the backing bass. Read the chord names before starting and play the lesson exercise for eight bars.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the bass example here without backing. Find the notes, mute spare strings and practise the phrase slowly. Add drums after the note order is secure.
cues.in-lab: Play the root and fifth of each displayed chord for eight bars at seventy BPM, with backing bass muted. Use even volume and controlled string crossings. Release between notes if needed rather than holding both frets continuously. Check the root whenever the chord changes.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: A wrong fifth may come from starting at the wrong root. Recheck G on E at fret three and D on A at fret five, then play each slowly.
cues.wrap: Practise root and fifth for five minutes at seventy BPM. Begin with G, then follow the backing chord changes for eight bars. Keep the backing bass muted. Next, add octaves.

cues.intro: In lesson forty one, you're going to alternate low and high G on bass and keep the other strings quiet as you cross between them.
cues.explain-a: Play G on E at fret three and G an octave higher on D at fret five. This moves two strings towards the thinner strings and two frets towards the bridge. On a standard four string bass, the same shape works from A to G.
cues.explain-b: Play lower G on a numbered beat and higher G on the following and. These are alternating quavers. Both notes are G, but they are different pitches. Keep the low note clear and control the unused strings.
cues.check: Play low G and high G separately, then alternate them without the track. Stop any spare strings ringing between notes.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with bass, G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock at seventy BPM. Mute the backing bass. Read the chord names before starting and play the lesson exercise for eight bars.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the bass example here without backing. Find the notes, mute spare strings and practise the phrase slowly. Add drums after the note order is secure.
cues.in-lab: Alternate octaves for eight bars at seventy BPM with backing bass muted. Follow the root when chords change. Mute unused strings and check even spacing and note endings. Release between notes or shift the hand rather than forcing an uncomfortable span.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: A missed octave can come from an unprepared string crossing. Find both G notes, look at the next position and practise one slow pair with muting before adding the beat.
cues.wrap: Practise alternating octaves for four minutes at seventy BPM, or slower initially. Check eight bars for even spacing and controlled endings. Next, walk towards a new chord.

cues.intro: In lesson forty two, you're going to play a four note walking line from G to C and land on C at the right chord and beat.
cues.explain-a: The example walks from G to C using G, A, B and C. On bass, use E at fret three, open A, A at fret two and A at fret three. Play one note per beat and check the order before adding backing.
cues.explain-b: A walking line must fit the harmony and arrival beat. Line up the final C with the chord and beat shown in the exercise. The four notes can be practised without backing first; their order alone doesn't show when the chords change.
cues.check: Play G, A, B and C without drums. Say C as the note you're heading towards before repeating the line.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with bass, G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock at seventy BPM. Mute the backing bass. Read the chord names before starting and play the lesson exercise for eight bars.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the bass example here without backing. Find the notes, mute spare strings and practise the phrase slowly. Add drums after the note order is secure.
cues.in-lab: Follow the chord-aligned walking exercise for eight bars at seventy BPM, with backing bass muted. Give each note a clear attack and ending. Check the arrival beat before starting. Don't rush from open A into the following notes.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: An early or late C means the arrival count needs work. Find the beat where C should land. Practise B to C against that count, then add G and A.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes at seventy BPM with the chord-aligned exercise. If only the four notes are shown, practise them without backing first. Next, study the drum pattern.

cues.intro: In lesson forty three, you're going to pick out the kick drum and line up chosen bass notes with its hits.
cues.explain-a: The kick is usually the low drum thump. The snare often gives a sharper sound, and the hi hat can mark smaller divisions of the beat. Listen to the pattern you hear rather than assuming the kick always plays the same beats.
cues.explain-b: Start with one G root on E at fret three. Choose a clear kick hit and join it. Not every bass note in every style has to copy the kick, but matching selected attacks is a useful way to learn how the two parts connect.
cues.check: Listen to one bar and pick out each kick hit without playing. Select one hit and place a G root with it.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with bass, G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock at seventy BPM. Mute the backing bass. Read the chord names before starting and play the lesson exercise for eight bars.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the bass example here without backing. Find the notes, mute spare strings and practise the phrase slowly. Add drums after the note order is secure.
cues.in-lab: Play eight bars at seventy BPM with the backing bass muted. Compare selected bass attacks with the kick and control note endings so they don't hide the next drum hit. Keep plucking pressure light and rest if tension develops.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: In Lock with the kick, tap the pulse and keep going through the silent section. Play through to the end of the game.
cues.success: Done. Next, check the bass notes against the kick drum.
cues.retry: Following the snare instead of the kick changes the alignment. Stop the bass, listen for the lower drum thump and tap it for a bar before adding one bass note.
cues.wrap: Practise with the kick for four minutes at seventy BPM. Play eight simple bars with the backing bass muted, then rest. Check note endings as well as attacks. Next, vary note length and space.

cues.intro: In lesson forty four, you're going to use note lengths and rests to support a bass groove, then compare it with one added sound.
cues.explain-a: Begin with roots on the beat. Let them speak clearly, then stop them cleanly. Compare a long note with a short one. Neither is always better. Choose the length that fits the groove and leaves the next attack easy to hear.
cues.explain-b: A ghost note is a muted, percussive sound without a clear new pitch. Rest the fretting fingers lightly on a string and pluck. If a harmonic rings, change the muting contact. Add one ghost note only after the basic line is steady.
cues.check: Play one bar of roots. Shorten the notes in the next bar and compare the space left between attacks.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab with bass, G, Major family, Ionian mode and rock at seventy BPM. Mute the backing bass. Read the chord names before starting and play the lesson exercise for eight bars.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use the bass example here without backing. Find the notes, mute spare strings and practise the phrase slowly. Add drums after the note order is secure.
cues.in-lab: Follow the chord changes for eight bars at seventy BPM, with backing bass muted. Keep the root clear before adding a fifth, octave or ghost note. Compare the line with and without the addition. Stop if the hands hurt and rest between attempts.
cues.back: Check what the exercise asks for. Repeat any part that still needs work before the next check.
cues.back-fallback: Return to the lesson part being practised. Review the example and repeat any unfinished section before continuing.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. Next, compare note lengths in the groove.
cues.retry: Extra notes can hide the pulse. Remove them, return to roots and use one even note length. Add one variation only after the basic line is steady.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes at seventy BPM. Compare a root line with one variation over eight bars. Keep the backing bass muted and follow the chords. Next, study music reading and rhythm.

cues.intro: In lesson one of level two, you're going to connect notation with the sound of C major.
cues.explain-a: Listen to C major before playing. Its notes are C, D, E, F, G, A and B. The next C repeats the tonic an octave higher. Listen to the semitone from B to C.
cues.explain-b: Notation shows pitch and rhythm. Tab shows strings and frets. Use both views to connect the page with the neck. Follow the displayed Shape two fingering without changing finger assignments or reaching back with the index finger.
cues.check: Play B, then C, using the diagram. Describe the change from the leading note to the tonic.
cues.to-lab: Open Mode Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Choose guitar. Use Shape two, root on A, both directions over one octave. Set eighty BPM. Play C Ionian over one octave at eighty BPM in both directions. Describe the final B to C movement.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Play B, then C, using the diagram. Describe the change from the leading note to the tonic.
cues.in-lab: If the ending doesn't sound settled, check that the final note is C, not B. Replay just those two notes. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.

cues.intro: In lesson four, you're going to read and clap note lengths.
cues.explain-a: In four four, with a crotchet beat, a semibreve lasts four beats, a minim two and a crotchet one. Two quavers fit into one beat. Four semiquavers fit into one beat.
cues.explain-b: An open notehead without a stem is a semibreve. Add a stem for a minim. Fill the head for a crotchet. Flags or beams shorten the value. Stem direction doesn't change the length.
cues.check: Clap one crotchet, two quavers, then four semiquavers. Keep each group inside one beat at sixty BPM.

cues.intro: In lesson five, you'll count bars in simple time.
cues.explain-a: A barline separates bars. In four four, each full bar holds four crotchet beats. Three four holds three, and two four holds two. Keep the pulse steady as the count returns to one.
cues.explain-b: The lower four names the crotchet unit. These metres divide each beat into two. Six eight works differently: six quavers normally form two dotted crotchet beats, not six equally strong beats.
cues.check: Count and clap one bar each of four four, three four and two four. Start the next bar without a gap.

cues.intro: This is lesson six. You're going to count silence as part of a rhythm.
cues.explain-a: A rest takes up time without a note. Match each rest to its note value. In four four with a crotchet beat, a crotchet rest takes one beat and a quaver rest half a beat.
cues.explain-b: Stop the strings for a rest rather than letting the previous note ring through it. A semibreve rest can also mean a whole bar of silence, even when the bar isn't four crotchet beats long.
cues.check: Clap beat one, stay silent on beat two, and clap three and four. Count all four beats.

cues.intro: In lesson seven, you're going to read dotted notes and ties.
cues.explain-a: A dot adds half the note's original length. With a crotchet beat, a dotted minim lasts three beats. A dotted crotchet lasts one and a half beats. Count the added time before playing.
cues.explain-b: A tie joins the same pitch. Sound the first note and hold it for both values added together. Don't pick again at the second notehead. A slur connects different pitches and isn't a tie.
cues.check: Count a dotted minim for three beats. Then hold two tied crotchets for two beats with one attack.

cues.intro: In lesson fourteen, you're going to measure tones and semitones.
cues.explain-a: One fret is a semitone. Two frets are a tone. Natural notes aren't evenly spaced: E to F and B to C are semitones. Most other neighbouring natural letters are a tone apart.

cues.intro: In lesson sixteen, you're going to read changes in volume and note attack.
cues.explain-a: Piano means soft and forte loud. Mezzo means moderately. Mezzo piano is moderately soft and mezzo forte moderately loud. A crescendo gets louder gradually; a diminuendo gets softer.

cues.intro: In lesson three, you're going to compare diminished and augmented triads.

cues.explain-b: The fifth is the main comparison after major and minor. Diminished lowers it; augmented raises it. Keep the spelling: C augmented uses G sharp, not A flat, because the outer interval is a fifth.
cues.check: Play C minor, then C diminished. Restore C major, then raise G to G sharp for C augmented.

cues.intro: In lesson four, you're going to name inversions from the bass note.
cues.explain-a: A chord's root names it; the bass note is the lowest note sounding. C, E and G with C lowest is root position. Put E lowest for first inversion, or G lowest for second inversion.
cues.explain-b: The chord stays C major because its notes stay C, E and G. Rearranging upper notes doesn't change the inversion unless the lowest note changes. Listen to the bass separately before naming the chord position.
cues.check: Play C major in root position, first inversion and second inversion. Say C, E or G for the bass.

cues.intro: In lesson five, you'll read a chord symbol before choosing a voicing.

cues.explain-b: An add nine chord adds a ninth without needing a seventh. A slash names the bass note after the chord: C over E keeps C major above E. Don't read every extra number as a new root.
cues.check: Spell C, C minor, C seven and C major seven. Play B flat and B separately to compare the sevenths.

cues.intro: This is lesson eighteen. You're going to read ninths, elevenths and thirteenths.

cues.intro: In lesson nineteen, you're going to compare added ninths with ninth chords.
cues.explain-a: C add nine uses C, E, G and D. C major nine adds D to C major seven, so it also contains B. C nine uses B flat instead. The ninth doesn't decide the seventh quality.

cues.explain-a: Build a short melody mostly from steps, with a few deliberate leaps. After a large leap, try stepping back in the opposite direction. This keeps the range controlled and the line easier to sing.
cues.explain-b: Create a phrase that pauses away from tonic, then a reply that ends on tonic. The two phrases can share rhythm or a short motif. The ending note works with the chord underneath, not in isolation.

cues.intro: In lesson twenty three, you're going to use passing notes and approaches to connect targets.
cues.explain-a: A passing note fills a stepwise gap. C, D, E uses D between C and E. An approach note comes just before a chosen target. A semitone approach can come from below or above.
cues.explain-b: Place the approach before the chord change and the target on the new chord's first beat. To reach G, F sharp can approach from below. It is outside C major but has a clear short term destination.

cues.intro: In lesson thirty two, you're going to compare natural minor and leading note progressions.

cues.intro: In lesson fifteen, you'll plan song sections and harmonic rhythm.
cues.explain-a: Form is the order of sections. Write an intro, verses, chorus, bridge and ending before arranging instruments. Mark each section's bar count and which material repeats. A different lyric doesn't always mean a new musical section.
cues.explain-b: Harmonic rhythm is how often chords change, not how busy the strumming is. Compare one chord per bar with two per bar while keeping the pulse unchanged. Form gives that change a place in the larger song.
cues.check: Write a G major section plan. Clap one pulse while naming changes once per bar, then twice per bar.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set G Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Build the section plan in Backbone, then compare harmonic rhythm with the matching Jam card.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Write a G major section plan. Clap one pulse while naming changes once per bar, then twice per bar.
cues.in-lab: If the faster strum is labelled faster harmony, count actual chord changes. The rhythm can get busier while the chord stays fixed. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.

cues.intro: In lesson sixteen, you're going to separate musical roles with register and density.
cues.explain-a: Texture describes how parts fit. Monophony is one line; homophony is melody with accompaniment; polyphony has independent lines. Several instruments doubling one melody don't automatically create polyphony.
cues.explain-b: Listen separately to bass, drums and chord accompaniment. Bass anchors the low register, drums clarify the pulse and chord parts supply harmony and rhythm. Leave space for the melody instead of making every part play continuously in the same register.
cues.check: Mute one backing part at a time. Name what disappears, then restore it and reduce your own chord density.
cues.to-lab: Open Jam Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Choose rock. Use a four bar loop. Set the chord count to four. Use triad voicings. Make three mixer passes, then add your own clear triad accompaniment.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Mute one backing part at a time. Name what disappears, then restore it and reduce your own chord density.
cues.in-lab: If the melody is masked, remove an upper chord note or move the accompaniment lower without crowding the bass. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If the melody is masked, remove an upper chord note or move the accompaniment lower without crowding the bass. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use C Ionian rock, four bars, four chords and triad voicings. Make three mixer passes, then add your own clear triad accompaniment. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll keep two musical lines distinct.

cues.intro: In lesson seventeen, you're going to keep two musical lines distinct.
cues.explain-a: Two voices can move in parallel, similar, contrary or oblique motion. Contrary means opposite directions; oblique means one note stays while the other moves. Follow each voice as a melody, not only as a stack of chords.
cues.explain-b: Use common tones and small steps where they fit. In strict counterpoint, parallel perfect fifths and octaves reduce independence and are normally avoided. That convention doesn't make every parallel movement wrong in every style.
cues.check: Write a bass rising C, D, E under an upper line falling G, F, E. Play each line alone before combining them.
cues.to-lab: Open Chord Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Start on the second chord. Write and play two independent voices over four chords, checking every vertical interval.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Write a bass rising C, D, E under an upper line falling G, F, E. Play each line alone before combining them.
cues.in-lab: If both parts sound like one doubled line, change one direction or hold a note. Check the individual lines before adding more notes. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Open Chord Lab and tap Test me. Play the chord once on your instrument. One correct play passes the check. With no mic, tap the chord's notes instead. The five question warm up is optional.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If both parts sound like one doubled line, change one direction or hold a note. Check the individual lines before adding more notes. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use the D minor chord in C Ionian as a reference. Write and play two independent voices over four chords, checking every vertical interval. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll compare a melody with an alternative harmony.

cues.intro: This is lesson eighteen. You're going to compare a melody with an alternative harmony.
cues.explain-a: Keep a short melody unchanged and write its original chord tones under each held note. Choose one replacement chord that still supports the important melody note. Change one bar before reharmonising a whole phrase.
cues.explain-b: Compare the bass and guide tone movement as well as the chord symbol. A replacement can share melody notes yet change the function. Return to the tonic clearly and record both versions so the comparison uses the same melody and rhythm.
cues.check: Write two four bar harmonisations of one melody. Circle the changed chord and mark any melody note that becomes a tension.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. As a draft exercise, compare an original four bar phrase with one revised chord while keeping the melody fixed.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use a blank page for the draft. Write two four bar harmonisations of one melody. Circle the changed chord and mark any melody note that becomes a tension.
cues.in-lab: If the replacement clashes on a long note, check that note against the new chord. Change the voicing or choose a different replacement. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the draft and compare its written plan with the result. Mark the exact part that needs revision.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Compare the melody notes with both chord versions. Mark any clash or unclear resolution and revise that bar before extending the draft.
cues.success: Done. Next, review the draft notes.
cues.retry: If the replacement clashes on a long note, check that note against the new chord. Change the voicing or choose a different replacement. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use C Ionian in Song Lab. As a draft exercise, compare an original four bar phrase with one revised chord while keeping the melody fixed. Record one result to compare at the next session. Keep unresolved points marked for review.

cues.intro: In lesson nineteen, you're going to combine harmony, melody and form in a short project.
cues.explain-a: Plan a short C major piece with a clear tonic, two contrasting sections and a written chord sequence. Mark the bar counts first. Add a melody with named chord targets and a bass line that follows the harmony.
cues.explain-b: Use one device from the course only where its resolution is clear. Keep the original version beside any changed harmony. Capture pitches and durations in notation or tab and label the key, functions and important nonchord notes.
cues.check: Play each part separately, then compare the combined piece with the written form. Check every bar length and final tonic arrival.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Draft the section plan and chord chart, then capture a playable melody and bass part in Tab Lab.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Use a blank page for the draft. Play each part separately, then compare the combined piece with the written form. Check every bar length and final tonic arrival.
cues.in-lab: If the project is hard to follow, remove one device and simplify the rhythm. Recheck the form before adding more harmony. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the draft and compare its written plan with the result. Mark the exact part that needs revision.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Review the draft for clear form, correct bar lengths, accurate chord labels and playable parts. Mark unresolved points for revision before treating the project as finished.
cues.success: Done. Next, review the draft notes.
cues.retry: If the project is hard to follow, remove one device and simplify the rhythm. Recheck the form before adding more harmony. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use C Ionian in Song Lab. Draft the section plan and chord chart, then capture a playable melody and bass part in Tab Lab. Record one result to compare at the next session. Keep unresolved points marked for review.

lessons.title: Brainstorm: What, Why, When, Where, Who, How

cues.intro: In lesson one of level eight, you're going to turn a song idea into a clear outline.
cues.explain-a: Choose one idea and write brief notes on what happens, why it matters, when and where it happens, who is involved and how the situation changes. Use concrete details before trying to rhyme.
cues.explain-b: Pick one main viewpoint and one central event. A song can leave information out, but its draft needs a clear focus. Keep extra ideas on a separate page instead of forcing all of them into the opening verse.
cues.check: Write one sentence for the song's main idea. Underline the event and the person whose viewpoint carries it.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Use a C major Song Lab verse and fill a song sheet with the central idea, setting, viewpoint and working title.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Write one sentence for the song's main idea. Underline the event and the person whose viewpoint carries it.
cues.in-lab: If the outline describes several unrelated stories, choose one event and keep the others for another draft. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If the outline describes several unrelated stories, choose one event and keep the others for another draft. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use a C major Song Lab verse and fill a song sheet with the central idea, setting, viewpoint and working title. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll organise a song on one working sheet.

cues.intro: In lesson two, you're going to organise a song on one working sheet.
cues.explain-a: A song sheet gathers the title, writers, key, metre, tempo, sections, chords and lyrics. Use a working title when the final one isn't clear. Record the key that actually sounds, especially if guitar shapes use a capo.
cues.explain-b: Keep writer contributions and proposed shares beside the draft, but don't treat an unagreed note as a signed agreement. Record section order and bar counts so the next session can start from the same version.
cues.check: Add a title, key and section order. Check that the chord chart and lyric headings use the same section names.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Fill the song sheet and mark any decisions still to be made.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Add a title, key and section order. Check that the chord chart and lyric headings use the same section names.
cues.in-lab: If the sheet mixes versions, date the current draft and keep earlier material separately. Match its title and section labels. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If the sheet mixes versions, date the current draft and keep earlier material separately. Match its title and section labels. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use C Ionian, four four, with a verse in Song Lab. Fill the song sheet and mark any decisions still to be made. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll generate lyric material without editing it immediately.

cues.intro: In lesson three, you're going to generate lyric material without editing it immediately.
cues.explain-a: Freewriting means writing continuously for a set time before editing. Use a specific topic and keep the pen or keyboard moving. The first pass gathers material rather than producing a finished lyric.
cues.explain-b: Object writing narrows the focus to one object and its sensory associations. Describe texture, sound, smell, movement and setting. Afterwards, select useful details and reshape them into lines instead of copying the whole paragraph into the song.
cues.check: Write for five minutes about one ordinary object. Afterwards, underline three concrete details that could belong in a verse.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Use a C major Song Lab verse as the writing page. Add selected freewriting details to the song sheet without treating the first pass as final lyrics.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Write for five minutes about one ordinary object. Afterwards, underline three concrete details that could belong in a verse.
cues.in-lab: If writing stops for every rhyme, leave rhyming until the next pass. Continue with ordinary sentences and sensory details. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If writing stops for every rhyme, leave rhyming until the next pass. Continue with ordinary sentences and sensory details. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use a C major Song Lab verse as the writing page. Add selected freewriting details to the song sheet without treating the first pass as final lyrics. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll try different entry points for a song.

lessons.title: Different Ways to Start a Song

cues.intro: In lesson four, you're going to try different entry points for a song.
cues.explain-a: A song can start from a title, a lyric scene, a chord pattern, a rhythm or a melodic phrase. Begin with the material already available rather than waiting for every part to arrive at once.
cues.explain-b: A title first draft needs a scene that supports the title. A music first draft needs words whose stress fits the phrase. A story first draft needs a central point, not every detail of the event.
cues.check: Make two short starts from the same idea: one title with a verse outline, then one four bar musical phrase.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Use a C major Song Lab verse. Record the chosen starting idea and add a second entry point to the song sheet for comparison.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Make two short starts from the same idea: one title with a verse outline, then one four bar musical phrase.
cues.in-lab: If one starting point stalls, keep its usable material and try another. Don't discard a workable phrase because the lyric isn't ready. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If one starting point stalls, keep its usable material and try another. Don't discard a workable phrase because the lyric isn't ready. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use a C major Song Lab verse. Record the chosen starting idea and add a second entry point to the song sheet for comparison. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll reduce a blocked writing task to one clear action.

cues.intro: In lesson five, you'll reduce a blocked writing task to one clear action.
cues.explain-a: Separate generating from judging. Choose one action, such as writing two concrete lines, playing four chords or finding a short melody. A limited task gives a draft something specific to work with.
cues.explain-b: Change the entry point if the current one produces no material. Move from words to rhythm, or from chords to a spoken line. Keep any useful result. A short break can help, but leave a written next step for returning.
cues.check: Write one scene in two plain lines without rhyme. Then speak the lines over a steady pulse.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Use a C major Song Lab verse. Add one usable two line idea to the song sheet and note the next writing step.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Write one scene in two plain lines without rhyme. Then speak the lines over a steady pulse.
cues.in-lab: If the lines stay abstract, name a place, an object and an action. Use those details before searching for polished wording. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.

cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use a C major Song Lab verse. Add one usable two line idea to the song sheet and note the next writing step. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll use a constraint to narrow a writing task.

cues.intro: This is lesson six. You're going to use a constraint to narrow a writing task.
cues.explain-a: A constraint limits one choice, such as four lines, three chords or a melody within five notes. It gives the exercise a clear boundary. Keep other choices open so the result can still vary.
cues.explain-b: Choose a constraint that can be checked. Four lines with one repeated phrase is clearer than an instruction to make the song interesting. Write a complete short draft within the limit before deciding whether to change it.
cues.check: Choose two chords and write a four bar phrase using only five melody notes. Mark each note as it appears.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Use a C major Song Lab verse. Put the constraint on the song sheet and write a short draft that follows it.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Choose two chords and write a four bar phrase using only five melody notes. Mark each note as it appears.
cues.in-lab: If the constraint stops every idea, loosen one part only. Keep the bar count while changing the note limit, for example. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If the constraint stops every idea, loosen one part only. Keep the bar count while changing the note limit, for example. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use a C major Song Lab verse. Put the constraint on the song sheet and write a short draft that follows it. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll map the roles and order of song sections.

cues.intro: In lesson seven, you're going to map the roles and order of song sections.
cues.explain-a: Verses develop the story with changing details. A chorus returns to the central message and often the title. A pre chorus can prepare the chorus, while a bridge adds contrast or another angle.
cues.explain-b: An intro prepares the opening sound and an outro shapes the ending. Section names describe a role, not a compulsory list. Mark repeated music separately from changing words and count the bars of each section.
cues.check: Write the section order of a song you know. Mark where the main repeated message returns and where new story details appear.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Use a C major Song Lab verse as the starting section. Map a complete song form with section names, order and bar counts.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Write the section order of a song you know. Mark where the main repeated message returns and where new story details appear.
cues.in-lab: If every lyric change becomes a chorus, compare the section's job. New details usually belong to verses; the repeated central message often marks the chorus. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If every lyric change becomes a chorus, compare the section's job. New details usually belong to verses; the repeated central message often marks the chorus. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use a C major Song Lab verse as the starting section. Map a complete song form with section names, order and bar counts. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll make a short hook easy to recognise.

cues.intro: In lesson eight, you're going to make a short hook easy to recognise.
cues.explain-a: A hook is a memorable repeated feature. It can be a sung title, rhythmic phrase or instrumental riff. Keep its main shape short enough to repeat clearly without depending on the whole verse for meaning.
cues.explain-b: Place the hook where the section gives it focus, often at the start or end of a chorus. Repetition works best when the phrase is easy to say or play. Change the surrounding material before changing the hook itself.
cues.check: Write a short title phrase and speak it twice with the same rhythm. Try one longer note on its main stressed word.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Use the C major Song Lab section to place a hook within the form. Mark each return rather than adding unrelated hooks to every line.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Write a short title phrase and speak it twice with the same rhythm. Try one longer note on its main stressed word.
cues.in-lab: If the phrase contains several competing ideas, remove extra words and keep one image or action. Retest its rhythm. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If the phrase contains several competing ideas, remove extra words and keep one image or action. Retest its rhythm. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use the C major Song Lab section to place a hook within the form. Mark each return rather than adding unrelated hooks to every line. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll compare verse chorus and A A B A forms.

cues.intro: In lesson nine, you're going to compare verse chorus and A A B A forms.
cues.explain-a: Verse chorus form alternates changing story sections with a returning central message. A bridge can contrast with both. Write the order before choosing the length of every section.
cues.explain-b: A A B A form returns to the A section around a contrasting B section. A common version uses four eight bar sections, but not every example has that length. A repeated A section isn't automatically a separate chorus.
cues.check: Draw one verse chorus map and one A A B A map. Mark the repeated material and the contrasting section.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Use C major Song Lab to map the two forms. Choose one for the current draft and label every section's bar count.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Draw one verse chorus map and one A A B A map. Mark the repeated material and the contrasting section.
cues.in-lab: If A A B A is labelled verse chorus only because A repeats, check the roles. Repetition alone doesn't define a chorus. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If A A B A is labelled verse chorus only because A repeats, check the roles. Repetition alone doesn't define a chorus. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use C major Song Lab to map the two forms. Choose one for the current draft and label every section's bar count. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll label and use rhyme schemes.

cues.intro: In lesson ten, you'll label and use rhyme schemes.
cues.explain-a: Assign a letter to each new line ending sound. If the first two lines rhyme and the next two use another rhyme, the scheme is A A B B. Alternate rhymes give A B A B.
cues.explain-b: Judge the spoken sound, not the spelling. Day and play rhyme even though their opening letters differ. Keep the meaning clear when choosing the rhyme. A rhyme shouldn't force the singer to say something the scene doesn't support.
cues.check: Write four line endings for A B A B, then read them aloud and check the two pairs by sound.
cues.to-lab: Open Song Lab. Set C Ionian, Major family. Use four four time. Use a C major Song Lab verse. Write a verse and chorus lyric with the chosen schemes marked beside the line endings.
cues.to-lab-fallback: Stay on this screen and use the lesson example. Write four line endings for A B A B, then read them aloud and check the two pairs by sound.
cues.in-lab: If a line exists only to reach a rhyme, rewrite its meaning first. Then find a word that fits both the sound and the scene. Keep the instrument supported and the wrist comfortable. Stop if there is pain or tingling.
cues.back: Return to the lesson example and compare it with your result. Note the exact bar, note or answer that still needs work.
cues.back-fallback: Open this lesson again and return to the example being practised. Keep your notes and continue from that part.
cues.quiz: Start the check. It has five questions. Get every answer right to pass. A missed question stays until you get it right.
cues.success: Done. You passed the check. Next, the wrap up.
cues.retry: If a line exists only to reach a rhyme, rewrite its meaning first. Then find a word that fits both the sound and the scene. Repeat that part before another full attempt.
cues.wrap: Practise for five minutes. Use a C major Song Lab verse. Write a verse and chorus lyric with the chosen schemes marked beside the line endings. Record one result to compare at the next session. Next, you'll replace general statements with concrete detail.

cues.intro: In lesson eleven, you're going to replace general statements with concrete detail.
cues.explain-a: A general line names an emotion or idea directly. A concrete line shows an action, object or sensory detail. Replace a statement such as being lonely with a scene that allows the listener to infer it.
cues.explain-b: Choose details that belong to this character and setting. A chorus may state the main idea plainly while the verses supply images. Not every line needs a detailed description; the balance should keep the story understandable.

lessons.title: The Two Copyrights in Every Song

cues.intro: In lesson twenty seven, you're going to separate the musical work from its recording.
cues.explain-a: The musical work is the song: its music and any lyrics. A sound recording captures one performance of it. The same song can have several recordings, each with its own ownership arrangements.
cues.explain-b: In Australia, copyright in an original protected work generally arises when it is fixed in material form, without a copyright registration fee. Writing shares, recording ownership and later licences still need clear agreements. This overview isn't individual legal advice.
